claims.text: A high-temperature solution anneal followed by rapid quenching will refine the dual-phase microstructure of high-entropy-alloy intermediate layers.
The treatment will enhance intrinsic heat-transfer capability without compromising structural integrity under high-temperature mechanical loading.
Current high-entropy-alloy intermediate layers have a dual-phase microstructure optimized for strength.
Current high-entropy-alloy intermediate layers have suboptimal heat-transfer connectivity.
A high-temperature solution anneal will homogenize the alloy and dissolve coarse precipitates.
Rapid quenching will retain a fine dual-phase microstructure with continuous heat-conduction paths.
The proposed improvement should hold at approximately 800–1000°C under reactor-relevant thermal and mechanical loading.
A fine dual-phase microstructure promotes continuous conductive pathways.
A high density of beneficial precipitates and grain boundaries helps retain strength.
Coarse phases act as heat-transfer barriers and their dissolution improves thermal transport.
Rapid quenching preserves a refined dual-phase structure that enhances thermal conductivity.
The treatment prevents excessive grain coarsening and enables effective load transfer among phases, thereby maintaining or improving strength.
The treated alloy will have higher thermal conductivity than the current intermediate-layer material.
The treated alloy will retain adequate mechanical integrity at the stated operating temperatures and loads.
Existing high-entropy-alloy intermediate layers prioritize structural strength but have limited thermal conduction at reactor operating conditions.
Performance outside 800–1000°C or in alloys with substantially different phase constituents is uncertain.
The magnitude of the conductivity enhancement and the treatment's effect on long-term microstructural stability remain unquantified.

The hypothesis is falsified if treated samples lack a statistically significant thermal-conductivity improvement or show any mechanical-performance degradation relative to composition-matched controls.
